div.head: Chapter 22
div.p: And because those who from these same invaders and raiders of foreign kingdoms — and properly tyrants — bought and have bought the Indians that they so unjustly made slaves: all those who today are and remain in the Indies knew, and had knowledge of this, and barely one will be found who did not have it, as to how they were made slaves through the aforesaid injustices. And of this there is a most efficacious and clear proof: that by command of the king, many years ago, it was generally commanded throughout all the Indies that they be placed in their liberty. And all those who come here to Castile before the King's Council to request their liberty are given it without delay or any proof whatsoever, it being most notorious that all those who made them slaves were flagrant man-stealers. And so, in buying them from those man-stealers or by any other means holding them as slaves, and for the whole time they had them and in selling them or giving them freely, they always had bad faith and were in mortal sin.

Likewise, because the merchants involved and have involved themselves of their own free will, solely out of their greed for the incomparable riches that the merchandise they carried and carry promised them, especially at a time when the Spaniards were and are waging those wars against those peoples without their prince moving them, summoning them, or commanding it of them, and they took no care to inform themselves from learned and God-fearing men of the truth, the clamors raised at court over this cause being so notorious, and in Spain the disputes of the learned and the sermons of the preachers, all of which was directed toward condemning as wrong — or at least as doubtful — what was being perpetrated in the Indies, as has been declared. And likewise the cruel deeds, so evil in themselves, that were done in the wars in which they themselves lived or their companions and perpetrators were found and assisted, of whose justice they ought at least to have doubted; and if they wish to confess the truth, they themselves judged those deeds as abominable. Which they could and should have known from the character of the time and of the persons and of their greed, and of the tyrants'; and in all probability their conscience told them — or should have told them — that these were deeds against justice and natural reason, as has been proved. All of which notwithstanding, they threw themselves headlong with eyes shut to carrying arms of every kind — especially horses, which do the greatest harm to those naked peoples, as was said — and many other things that aided the iniquitous subjection and destruction of those kingdoms; especially in New Spain, when the first tyrant and the tyrants entered it and subjugated it, and far worse and more so in the kingdoms of Peru, where all the evils have been committed doubled and trebled and a thousand times over, and from which the greatest and unheard-of treasures have been stolen; and the merchants for the most part have taken their share. Therefore they were and are guilty of all the mortal sins that the tyrants committed in the wars, of killings and despoilings and robberies and usurpations of the natural lords, and are bound to make restitution for everything stolen, in solidum, because they were the ones who most aided in the wars to the harm and destruction of those peoples, the natural lords of those lands, with their merchandise, sustaining those who so unjustly ravaged and laid waste those innocent peoples. Such that, even if they had carried merchandise not for profit but as alms to those who were in extreme need, the merchants would have sinned mortally even if they supplied them with things that were not weapons but only food and provisions, while they were carrying out the deeds they did; on the contrary, they should have cut off all sustenance from them if they could, so that they would stop. The reason is that we are obliged both to help our neighbors by doing good, and also to prevent all evil from them by every possible means: "There is not much difference between inflicting death and allowing it. For it is proved that one who, when he is able to prevent it, does not prevent it, inflicts death upon those who are languishing." 83 dist., at the opening; and on this much has been written; and thus not even alms — though they perished of hunger — could be given to them without mortal sin. The reason is that, since they were persevering in such works, those who gave such things were participants in those evils and harms. And on this there is authority in Holy Scripture, Ecclesiasticus 12: "Do good to the humble, and give not to the ungodly. Forbid him to be given bread, lest he become thereby more powerful than you. For the Most High abhors sinners, and will render vengeance to the ungodly." And in the canons there is registered a sentence of Saint Augustine in the Letter to Vincentius the Donatist, 5, q. 5, c. non omnis: "It is more useful to take bread from the hungry man who, secure in his food, neglects justice, than to break bread with the hungry man so that, seduced by injustice, he may consent to it." Thus far he. And Saint Thomas, to the point, in Opusculum 19, cap. 7, column 17, ad 4m, says: "How much more should alms be withheld from those who ask for them, when from what they receive they manifestly take occasion for injustice." Thus far he.

It appears, then, that such merchants never had good faith but bad conscience, in carrying the said merchandise even when it was not weapons. And neither ignorance nor doubt could excuse them, since they are in all things more astute than others and know first the things that pass at court and were passing in the Indies; and they are even the first to receive news of the affairs of the world, and even the kings do not learn the news so quickly.

And so, by everything said, this eighth principle appears to be true; namely, that no Spaniard of those who have passed to the Indies, in the fifty years up to this year of 1563 in which by the mercy of God we now live, among those who have been found — little or much — in the destruction and ruin of those Indian peoples and lands, has had or has good faith with respect to four things. The first, with respect to the wars.
The second, with respect to the armed expeditions and raids — which are all one with the wars — that they called entradas and rancherías.
The third, with respect to purchasing the Indian slaves taken in them, those who bought them from the very ones who made them slaves.
The fourth, with respect to the merchandise that was carried and sold to those who waged and carried on the said wars, etc.
